t: Introduction: aim of the session and plan
n: In this session we study the topic of mechanical asphyxia. Mechanical asphyxia means disturbance of external respiration under the action of an external mechanical factor, with development of oxygen deficiency in the body. Fulminant and acute hypoxia caused by external action is often encountered as an object of forensic medical examination. In the forensic medical classification there are three kinds of mechanical asphyxia: from compression, from obstruction, and asphyxia in a confined space. The plan is as follows: classification of hypoxia, course of asphyxia, post-asphyxial state, general signs, then hanging, drowning and other kinds.

t: The concept of oxygen and hypoxia
n: First let us consider the concept of oxygen and hypoxia. Of the oxygen the body needs, 98.5-99.0% is obtained through the respiratory organs, and the rest through the skin, stomach and intestines. At rest, 6-8 litres of air per minute are required. In physical exertion this requirement may rise up to 10-20 times. Hypoxia is oxygen deficiency, which disturbs metabolism in the tissues. The sensitivity of tissues varies and depends on phylogenetic age. If tissue respiration in the central nervous system stops for 5-10 minutes, the changes are irreversible. In muscle and connective tissue this period is considerably longer.

t: Classification of hypoxia: exogenous and endogenous
n: Now the classification of hypoxia. Hypoxia is divided into exogenous and endogenous states; the classification is given according to Yu.I. Pigolkin (2012). There are three types of exogenous hypoxia. In the hypoxic type the inspired mixture is low in oxygen, whereas normally air contains 20.93% oxygen. An example is mountain or altitude sickness. In the hyperoxic type there is a lot of oxygen and it acts for a long time, and changes develop in the lungs. In the hypercapnic type oxygen decreases and carbon dioxide increases; this is seen in a confined closed space. The endogenous types: respiratory, haemic, circulatory, cytotoxic and physiological; they are considered separately below.

t: Types of endogenous hypoxia
n: Let us consider the types of endogenous hypoxia. Respiratory hypoxia is related to lung function and has direct and indirect forms. It is caused by obstruction of the airways and compression of the neck. In circulatory hypoxia the circulation is disturbed. In haemic hypoxia haemoglobin in the blood decreases or its binding of oxygen is disturbed; poisoning may also be the cause. In cytotoxic hypoxia tissue respiration is disturbed. Physiological hypoxia is often temporary: for example, during physical exertion or when a large amount of food is eaten at once. That is, the endogenous types are distinguished by internal causes in the body.

t: Rate of development of hypoxia
n: Hypoxia is also classified by the rate of development. Four types are distinguished according to speed of development. Fulminant hypoxia develops in seconds. Acute hypoxia develops in minutes. The subacute form develops over hours, and the chronic form over days, weeks and months. For forensic medicine, fulminant and acute hypoxia are important. This is because such states, caused by external action, are often encountered as an object of examination. Remember: types measured in hours and months are of less significance in forensic medical examination.

t: Case analysis: determining the type of hypoxia
n: Now a case analysis: we determine the type of hypoxia. In the first situation the person has lost blood, haemoglobin in the blood has decreased, and the airways are open. Which type of hypoxia is this? In the second situation, because of poisoning, the tissues cannot utilise oxygen; tissue respiration is disturbed. Which type is this? Answer: the first is haemic hypoxia, the second cytotoxic, that is, tissue hypoxia. Note: hypercapnic hypoxia is not the same as haemic hypoxia. The hypercapnic type is exogenous: in enclosed air oxygen decreases and carbon dioxide increases. The haemic type, by contrast, is endogenous and is related to the blood.

t: The concept of asphyxia and mechanical asphyxia
n: We move on to the concept of asphyxia. The word asphyxia comes from Greek: "a" is a negation, and "sphygmos" is pulse. The original meaning is absence of pulse. In forensic medicine oxygen deficiency is designated by this term. Asphyxia is a decrease of oxygen and an increase of carbon dioxide in the body due to disturbance of external respiration. As a result the activity of vital systems is acutely disturbed. Attention: hypoxia and asphyxia are not the same. In asphyxia, hypoxia, that is, oxygen deficiency, develops together with hypercapnia, that is, excess CO₂. A state arising from disturbance of external respiration under the action of a mechanical factor is called mechanical asphyxia.

t: Classification of mechanical asphyxia
n: Let us consider the classification of mechanical asphyxia. In the forensic medical classification three kinds are distinguished: from compression, from obstruction, and asphyxia in a confined space. Asphyxia from compression is of two kinds. In the strangulation type the neck is compressed, and in the compression type the chest and abdomen. Attention: do not confuse these two. In asphyxia from obstruction the respiratory openings and passages are closed, and drowning also belongs here. In a confined space, asphyxia in an enclosed environment develops. In addition there are cases of autoerotic asphyxia, that is, sexual asphyxia.

t: Autoerotic asphyxia (sexual asphyxia)
n: On autoerotic asphyxia, that is, sexual asphyxia. This phenomenon is seen more often in solitary middle-aged men inclined to sexual deviations, and sometimes in young men. Sexual arousal occurs under conditions of hypoxia and hypercapnia. Orgasm occurs in the state of asphyxia spontaneously or as a result of masturbation. A characteristic feature is that the asphyxial process is regulated by the hand, foot or devices. Mainly the neck is compressed with a noose, or a confined environment is created with a polyethylene bag.

t: Autoerotic asphyxia (sexual asphyxia) (continued)
n: We continue with the topic of autoerotic asphyxia. If such a state ends in death, it is assessed as an accident. At the scene, pornographic pictures, imitations of genitalia and clothing of the other sex are found. The corpse may also be naked. That is, in assessing such a state, attention is paid to these signs at the scene.

t: Course of asphyxia: pre-asphyxial and asphyxial periods
n: We move on to the course of asphyxia: the pre-asphyxial and asphyxial periods. The pre-asphyxial period lasts on average 20-30 seconds. Breathing is briefly held, then its rhythm slows. The body adapts: the quantity of blood increases, the blood becomes thinner and is redistributed to vital organs. For this reason signs of asphyxia do not develop in this period. If the asphyxial action continues, the asphyxial period begins. It consists of five stages: inspiratory dyspnoea, expiratory dyspnoea, brief pause, terminal breathing and complete arrest. The brief pause lasts 30-40 seconds, and terminal breathing up to 5 minutes. In complete arrest the respiratory centre is paralysed.

t: Stages of inspiratory and expiratory dyspnoea
n: Let us compare the stages of inspiratory and expiratory dyspnoea. In the inspiratory stage, inspiration becomes quicker and longer, pleural pressure falls sharply, arterial pressure falls and venous pressure rises, and the pulse slows. In this stage consciousness is lost after 40-60 seconds; the stage lasts about a minute. In the expiratory stage, expiration is forceful and prolonged, pleural pressure rises, arterial pressure rises and venous pressure falls, and the pulse quickens. In this stage there may be strong clonic convulsions with discharge of urine, semen and faeces. Attention: it is necessary to distinguish injury from striking during convulsions from injury inflicted by another person.

t: Final stages and mechanism of death
n: Let us consider the final stages and the mechanism of death. The brief pause lasts 30-40 seconds: from excess carbon dioxide the vagus nerve is stimulated, breathing stops, and reflexes begin to fade. Terminal breathing lasts up to 5 minutes: there is occasional irregular breathing, often with opening of the mouth; at the end arterial pressure falls extremely low. In complete arrest the respiratory centre is paralysed. The heart may beat for another 3-10 minutes, then the heart stops and clinical death occurs. If reflex cardiac arrest occurs within 30 seconds, asphyxial signs do not develop. Minovici carried out a hanging experiment on himself in 1905.

t: Case analysis and quick question: course of asphyxia
n: Case analysis and quick question. Situation: 40-60 seconds after the onset of asphyxia consciousness is lost; breathing has become faster and longer, the pulse is slow, and venous pressure is raised. Which stage is this? It is the inspiratory stage. In the next stage expiration strengthens, and clonic convulsions and discharge of urine and faeces are observed. Distinguish injury from convulsions from injury inflicted by another person. Quick question: if the heart stopped reflexly within 30 seconds, why may signs of asphyxia not be found on the corpse? Answer: the general asphyxial signs do not have time to develop. Attention: arterial pressure falls in the inspiratory stage and rises in the expiratory stage.

t: Post-asphyxial state and its periods
n: The post-asphyxial state and its periods. If asphyxia ends without death, the set of changes that has arisen is called the post-asphyxial state. The signs depend on the type of asphyxial action, its duration and the health of the organism. In mild cases, with full help, the changes disappear without trace in 1-2 weeks. The post-asphyxial state consists of four periods: the first is asphyxial coma, the second stupor, the third disorientation and amnesia, and the fourth residual effects. These periods succeed one another in sequence.

t: Asphyxial coma and the period of stupor
n: Let us consider asphyxial coma and the period of stupor. At the beginning of coma the muscles are atonic, the pupils dilated, reflexes cannot be elicited; the brainstem centres are disturbed, and pressure is very low. After breathing and the heart are restored, decerebrate rigidity develops: pressure and muscle tone rise, tonic convulsions occur, and body temperature rises. In the last stage tonic-clonic convulsions and hyperkinesias are observed, and reflexes begin to recover; sometimes signs of internal bleeding are found. In stupor the victim emerges from coma and there are no convulsions: sopor, deep stupor, mild stupor, then drowsiness succeed one another in sequence.

t: Disorientation, residual effects and complications
n: On disorientation, residual effects and complications. Even when consciousness is restored, the person is confused in time and space. Confabulation is the filling of a memory gap with false memory without awareness of it; retrograde amnesia is also observed. With full medical help, mild changes pass without trace in 1-2 weeks. In other cases memory and attention are impaired, and headache, paralysis, and reduced vision and hearing remain. This means that the outcome depends on the severity of the asphyxia and on the help given.

t: Disorientation, residual effects and complications (continued)
n: We continue on complications. In the liver there are dystrophy and focal necrobiosis, and in the mucosa of the gastro-intestinal tract erosions and ulcers. As complications, organ failure, peritonitis and internal bleeding may develop. The cause also differs according to the time of death. In the first minutes and hours, death occurs from asphyxial coma. In the first day, death is from pulmonary and cerebral oedema, and later from hypostatic pneumonia.

t: Case analysis: a victim in the post-asphyxial state
n: Case analysis: a victim in the post-asphyxial state. Situation: a person who was drowning in water has been rescued. Consciousness is restored, there are no convulsions, but he is confused about the present time and place and does not remember the event. Question: which period of the post-asphyxial state is this? How does it differ from the period of stupor? Direction: this is the 3rd period, that is, disorientation and memory impairment. False memory, that is, confabulation, may fill the place of events that are not remembered. Remember: in a subsequent examination, complete medical documentation is very important for determining the severity of injury in a living person, and in the event of death for determining its cause.

t: General external signs of mechanical asphyxia
n: General external signs of mechanical asphyxia. Cyanosis of the face and neck arises from convulsions during dyspnoea, but it is not constant: depending on the position of the corpse it may disappear, or appear even without asphyxia. Cadaveric lividity, because of the fluid blood and saturation with carbon dioxide, is extensive, bluish-violet, and forms within 1 hour after death. Subconjunctival ecchymoses arise from a sharp change in blood pressure and are clearly seen in the transitional fold. Mydriasis in stress arises from the action of catecholamines and is an inconstant sign. In convulsions urine, faeces, semen and the mucous plug are discharged, because smooth muscles contract.

t: General internal signs
n: Let us consider the general internal signs. Asphyxial heart, anaemia and a contracted spleen are relatively pathognomonic, that is, characteristic, signs of mechanical asphyxia. In the asphyxial heart the right chambers are fuller of blood. The blood is fluid and dark red; this is due to hypercapnia and increased fibrinogenase. In the lungs partial emphysema appears in the stages of dyspnoea; the internal organs are venously congested. Tardieu spots form from raised pressure and permeability of the vessel wall, and are found more often between the lobes of the lung, on the diaphragmatic pleura and on the posterior surface of the heart. In Sabinsky's sign, blood from the depot is released in the pre-asphyxial period.

t: Case analysis and quick question: general signs
n: Case analysis and quick question. Case: on a corpse the face is bluish, the blood is fluid, there are Tardieu spots and a contracted spleen. Question: is this enough to say death was from asphyxia? These signs are non-specific: they also occur in electrical injury, anaphylactic shock and sudden cardiac death. Therefore the whole set is assessed. Asphyxial heart, anaemia and a contracted spleen are relatively pathognomonic, but they too are assessed together with other signs. Attention, there is a risk of error. Facial cyanosis is not proof of mechanical asphyxia: if the face of the corpse lies downward, bluishness occurs with other causes too.

t: Hanging: types and properties of the noose
n: Hanging: types and properties of the noose. The noose may be of soft material, for example a towel or scarf, semi-rigid, for example a rope or belt, or rigid, for example wire or chain. The ring may be single-, double- or multi-turn, slipping or non-slipping. The knot may indicate a professional skill; the noose is cut off on the side opposite the knot. Hanging is divided into two types. In typical hanging, the body hangs freely in the noose, and the knot is at the back of the neck. In atypical hanging, part of the body has support, and the knot lies in the front or side region.

t: Mechanism of death in hanging
n: The mechanism of death in hanging. The noose compresses the neck. As a result the base of the tongue is displaced and the airway narrows; complete closure occurs only in some cases. The veins are compressed, venous outflow is hindered, intracranial pressure rises, and brain function is disturbed. If the vagus nerve is stimulated, reflex cardiac arrest is possible; in heart disease this risk is high. The slide shows another factor: rupture of the spinal cord or disc. Consequently death does not occur from one factor but from the combined action of several.

t: Description of the strangulation furrow
n: Description of the strangulation furrow. The furrow has the appearance of an abrasion; its place, direction, width and depth are compared with the noose. In typical hanging the furrow is high, above the hyoid bone, obliquely vertical. In atypical hanging the furrow may be lower, and its verticality is reduced. The furrow also differs according to the type of noose. With a rigid noose the furrow on the skin is dense and deep, more distinct opposite the knot. With a soft noose the furrow is not very noticeable, but on internal examination a whitish band is found.

t: Internal signs in the neck and vitality of the furrow
n: Internal signs in the neck and vitality of the furrow. Signs of compression include the signs of Casper and Brouardel. Casper's is a whitish band in the soft tissue; Brouardel's is haemorrhage behind the larynx. Signs of stretching include the signs of Amussat, Martin, Walcher and Simon. Signs of stretching are seen mainly in obese persons in typical hanging with a jerk. Now the question of vitality of the furrow, that is, whether the furrow was formed during life. As a macroscopic sign, the Bokarius test, that is, a skin flap, is examined. Under the microscope, the signs of Neiding and Kasyanov are identified.

t: Ligature strangulation and manual strangulation
n: Let us compare ligature strangulation and manual strangulation. In ligature strangulation, the ligature is tightened not by body weight but by another force. This is often encountered in homicide. The furrow is horizontal and closed, usually located at the level of the thyroid cartilage or lower. There may be signs of struggle; the hyoid bone is not a typical injury, but a horn of the thyroid cartilage may be broken. Manual strangulation is usually a sign of homicide. In it there is no furrow, but there are finger marks: round bruises and fingernail abrasions. The horns of the hyoid bone may be broken, and internal injury is more extensive. Reflex cardiac arrest is observed more often here.

t: Blunt-object strangulation and positional asphyxia
n: Blunt-object strangulation and positional asphyxia. In strangulation with a blunt object, for example a stick or a chair back, the injuries lie in the projection of the contact surface: bruise, abrasion and internal haemorrhages. The hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage may also be injured. The nature of the injury depends on the object and the force of action. In positional asphyxia the head remains flexed forward or sideways for a long time, usually when an unconscious person falls into a confined space. In this case there is no strangulation furrow on the neck.

t: Blunt-object strangulation and positional asphyxia (continued)
n: We continue on positional asphyxia. The flexion fold on the neck may resemble a furrow. Therefore internal examination is carried out: in it a whitish band and haemorrhages are found. The diagnosis of positional asphyxia is made by excluding other causes of death. That is, other causes must first be ruled out.

t: Case analysis and quick question: strangulation
n: Case analysis and quick question: strangulation. Case: on the neck of the corpse there is a horizontal, closed furrow at the level of the thyroid cartilage. A horn of the cartilage is broken, and there are also signs of struggle on the body. Question: is this hanging or ligature strangulation? Note the place and direction of the furrow and the signs of stretching. Attention, there is a risk of error! In hanging, injury to the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage is not typical; it may occur if the noose is lower. Quick question: when are the signs of Amussat, Walcher and Simon absent? Answer: in ligature strangulation, because the neck is not stretched.

t: Obstructive asphyxia: respiratory openings and passages
n: Obstructive asphyxia: respiratory openings and passages. Closing the respiratory openings may be homicide, for example of a child or a weakened adult, or an accident, for example in an unconscious person. If there was no resistance, no characteristic signs are found. If there was resistance, there are bruising and abrasion around the mouth and nose and haemorrhage in the gum and oral mucosa. Fibres of a soft object may also be found. The airways are blocked by a foreign body, a granular substance, blood or vomit. Death often occurs because of difficulty in air reaching the lungs.

t: Obstructive asphyxia: respiratory openings and passages (continued)
n: We continue on obstructive asphyxia. In this case reflex spasm or cardiac arrest may also lead to death. Attention: finding vomit does not mean death from obstruction. Vomit gets in during resuscitation, transport and putrefaction too. But in that case it is in small amounts and is not found in the small bronchi. Consequently the amount and location of the vomit are decisive.

t: Drowning: true and asphyxial types
n: Drowning: true and asphyxial types. In true drowning, water reaches the alveoli. In asphyxial drowning, laryngeal spasm does not let water into the trachea and bronchi. In true drowning, persistent white foam, that is, Kruszewski foam, forms; water and foreign substances are found in the airways; there are Tardieu and Rasskazov-Lukomsky-Paltauf spots; and the stomach contains up to 300 ml of water. In asphyxial drowning, the foam is scanty and unstable, there is no water in the airways, only Tardieu spots are present, and the stomach contains up to 1 l of water. In sea water, the blood thickens and Rasskazov-Lukomsky-Paltauf spots do not form. In the asphyxial type, 5-15 ml of fluid is found in the cavity of the skull base; this is Sveshnikov's sign.

t: Determining the vitality of drowning
n: Determining the vitality of drowning. If diatom plankton is found in the parenchymatous organs and bone marrow, the drowning was vital; it must correspond to the water of the body of water. In the asphyxial type, skull-base fluid is taken for plankton; diatoms in the lung are not diagnostic. Pseudoplankton is identified by polarising microscopy; finding Pseudomonas confirms that the person entered the water alive. The order of examination is as follows: first a 1 l water sample is taken, then pieces of organs. Then diatom, bacterial and cryoscopic examinations are carried out. The results are compared with the water sample, and a conclusion on vitality is drawn.

t: Signs of a corpse's stay in water
n: Signs of a corpse's stay in water. Clothing and body are contaminated with mud, sand, oil and algae; a corpse cools faster in water. In cold water the skin pales and takes on a "goose-skin" appearance; if the water is warm, changes develop faster. By time: after a few hours the fingers pale; the palm changes in 2-5 days and the sole in 5-8 days; in 10-15 days the hair is easily pulled out; after 2-3 weeks the skin of the palm separates. Injuries occur from striking the bottom, parts of a vessel, fish, currents and during resuscitation, that is, revival.

t: Case analysis: a corpse recovered from water
n: Case analysis: a corpse recovered from water. Situation: a corpse has been taken out of the water; around the mouth and nose there is white fine-bubbled foam, and the lungs are doughy and of large volume. This corresponds to true drowning: foreign substances that entered with the water, that is, algae, silt and sand, are found in the airways. Attention: if the heart and breathing stop on entering the water, signs of asphyxia do not have time to develop; then changes in the heart are sought. Question: which laboratory examinations confirm that the corpse entered the water alive?

t: Compression asphyxia
n: Compression asphyxia. If the chest and abdomen are compressed by a blunt object and respiratory movements are restricted or stop, compression asphyxia develops. It is often encountered as a result of earthquakes, landslides, building collapses, vehicle overturns and crowd crushes. Frontal compression is more dangerous than lateral. When only the chest is compressed, death comes faster, whereas the body is more resistant to compression of the abdomen alone. Signs: swelling and bluishness of the face, haemorrhages on the face, neck and chest, that is, the ecchymotic mask; and also carmine pulmonary oedema.

t: Asphyxia in a confined enclosed environment
n: Asphyxia in a confined enclosed environment. In an enclosed environment oxygen gradually decreases and carbon dioxide rises. In death, the rise in the amount of carbon dioxide is of leading importance. If carbon dioxide in the air reaches 0.5%, breathing quickens. In adults death occurs at 8-10%, whereas in children 2.0-2.5% is dangerous to life. In homicide, a plastic bag is placed over the head. In autoerotic asphyxia there is also a bag method, and this state is classed as an accident. Examples of a not fully enclosed environment are a deep well, a silage pit and a vegetable store. Here, toxic substances released by fermentation and putrefaction also contribute to death.

t: Case analysis: compression and enclosed environment
n: Case analysis: compression and enclosed environment. First case: a crowd crush on leaving a stadium. In the corpse, swelling, bluishness and haemorrhages of the face are expected, that is, the "ecchymotic mask" or Olivier-Danger sign. If compression lasts long, the lungs swell and take on a bright red colour; this is "carmine oedema", that is, Lacassagne's sign. Frontal compression is more dangerous than lateral. Second case: a child has become trapped in a refrigerator compartment. In the corpse there will be only general asphyxial signs and signs of rapid death, and no change specific to this kind is found. Attention: in compression, mechanical injuries may be a competing cause of death, so differential diagnosis is carried out carefully.

t: Conclusions and consolidation
n: Conclusions and consolidation. Mechanical asphyxia is divided into three kinds: from compression, from obstruction, and asphyxia in a confined space. In asphyxia, hypoxia develops together with hypercapnia. General asphyxial signs are not specific; in diagnosis their whole set is taken. Asphyxial heart, anaemia and a contracted spleen are relatively pathognomonic. Distinction: in hanging the strangulation furrow, in true drowning Kruszewski foam, in compression the ecchymotic mask. In an enclosed environment there is no characteristic sign. Examination questions: vitality of the furrow and of entry into water, cause of death. Review question: which sign is general, and which is characteristic of the kind?
